--- title: "Data wrangling I" subtitle: "POL51" author: "Haley Daarstad" institute: "University of California, Davis" date: today date-format: long format: revealjs: chalkboard: true slide-number: true height: 900 width: 1600 code-line-numbers: true smooth-scrawl: true theme: [simple, html/custom.scss] incremental: true title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: img/dubois-spiral-2.png data-background-size: contain data-background-position: right data-background-color: "#dc354a" --- # Plan for today {.center background-color="#dc354a"} Review Data Visualization . . . Wrangling and pipes . . . Subsetting data ## Graph 4: the barplot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-3_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: . . . Barplots place a *category* (place, country, person, etc) on one axis and a *quantity* (amount, average, median, etc.) on another . . . Useful for making **comparisons**, highlighting **differences** Why would there be differences across TV consumption? ## The grammar of barplots ::::::: columns :::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: The data |marital | tv| |:-------------|----:| |No answer | 2.56| |Never married | 3.11| |Separated | 3.55| |Divorced | 3.09| |Widowed | 3.91| ::: ::: ::: :::: :::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Mapping the data |Data |Aesthetic |Geometry | |:-------|:---------|:----------| |tv |x |geom_col() | |marital |y |geom_col() | ::: ::: ::: :::: :::::::
. . . You could switch the x and y mapping around, but I think categories look better on the y-axis ## The barplot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(tv, aes(y = marital, x = tv)) + geom_col() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-3_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Graph 5: the boxplot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-3_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: . . . Boxplots compare **distributions** of *continuous* variables across groups they show us *more* than the barplot which only gives us a quantity for each group ## Compare distributions: the boxplot ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} Boxplots contain a lot of info 🥵: - bold line is the **median** observation - box is the **middle** 50% of observations - thin lines show you min and max value, *except...* - the dots, which are **outlier** observations ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-3_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::::: interpret ## The grammar of boxplots ::::::: columns :::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: The data |continent | lifeExp| |:---------|-------:| |Asia | 43.83| |Europe | 76.42| |Africa | 72.30| |Africa | 42.73| |Americas | 75.32| ::: ::: ::: :::: :::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Mapping the data |Data |Aesthetic |Geometry | |:--------|:---------|:--------------| |contient |y |geom_boxplot() | |lifeExp |x |geom_boxplot() | ::: ::: ::: :::: :::::::
. . . You could switch the x and y mapping around, but I think categories look better on the y-axis ## The five(-ish) graphs ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Graph aes() geom_ Purpose
Scatterplot x = cause, y = effect point() Relationships
Time series x = date, y = variable line() Trends
Histogram x = cont. variable histogram() Distributions
Barplot y = category, x = quantity col() Compare amounts
Boxplot y = category, x = cont. variable boxplot() Compare distributions
````` ::: ::: . . . Know how and when to use which! # Making better graphs {background-color="#dc354a"} - We've barely scratched the surface; there's many more aesthetics, geometries, and layers in `ggplot()` - Here are some of my favorite ones - And some ideas for making graphs better ## Showing "movement" using panels ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-3_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: . . . We can use **panels** to show *movement* of a variable across time, space, etc. What is this graph showing us? ## Using facet_wrap ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = lifeExp)) + geom_histogram() + facet_wrap(vars(year)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-3_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: Make sure the facetting variable is wrapped in `vars()`! ## Make aesthetics static ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(gap_07, aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) + geom_point(size = 4, color = "orange", shape = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-3_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: Take your aesthetics out of `aes()` and into `geom()` to make them *static* ## Use different color and fill scales ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = lifeExp, fill = continent)) + geom_histogram() + scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-3_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: `scale_fill_brewer()` for `fill`, `scale_color_brewer` for `color` ## My favorite scale (right now) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = lifeExp, fill = continent)) + geom_histogram() + scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "magma") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-3_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: `scale_fill_viridis_d` for *discrete* variables, `scale_fill_viridis_d` for continuous ## Many other themes ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-3_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: `theme_spongeBob()` from `tvthemes` package, many more online # Review {background-color="#dc354a"} ::: incremental - Scatterplots? [`geom_point()`: two continuous variables (x and y)]{.fragment} - Time series? [`geom_line()`: one time/date variable (x) + one continuous variable (y)]{.fragment} - Histograms? [`geom_histogram()`: one continuous variable (x)]{.fragment} - Barplots? [`geom_col()`: one categorical variable (x) + one continuous variable (y, already summarized)]{.fragment} - Boxplots? [`geom_boxplot()`: one continuous variable (y), often split by one categorical variable (x)]{.fragment} ::: ## What is data-wrangling? . . . > ...the process of transforming and mapping data from one "raw" data form into another format with the intent of making it more appropriate and valuable for a variety of downstream purposes such as analytics... **Data analysts typically spend the majority of their time in the process of data wrangling compared to the actual analysis of the data.** -- Wikipedia . . . Most of your time working with data will be spent **wrangling** it into a usable form for analysis ## Pipes: connecting data to functions ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} directors_profit = movies |> # only look at horror movies filter(genre1 == "Horror" | genre2 == "Horror" | genre3 == "Horror") |> # calculate profit mutate(profit = gross - budget) ``` :::
You've seen these before... ## What are pipes? ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} - **Pipes** link **data** to **functions** - They look like this `%>%`, or `|>` - Definitely use keyboard shortcuts - OSX: Cmd + Shift + M - Windows: Ctrl + Shift + M ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](img/pipes.png) ::: ::::: ## Why pipes? . . . With pipes: 😍 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins %>% filter(species == "Adelie") %>% mutate(body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000) %>% select(body_mass_kg) ``` ::: . . . Without pipes: 🤢 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} select(mutate(filter(penguins, species == "Adelie"), body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000), body_mass_kg) ``` ::: . . .
Both produce the same output, but pipes make code more **legible** ## Making sense of pipes: "and then..." ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} directors_profit = movies %>% # only look at horror movies filter(genre1 == "Horror" | genre2 == "Horror" | genre3 == "Horror") %>% # calculate profit mutate(profit = gross - budget) ``` ::: . . .
You can read the pipe as if it said "*and then*"... . . . 1. Take the data object `movies`, AND THEN 2. `filter` so genre1, genre2, or genre3 equal HORROR, AND THEN 3. `mutate` so that... # Subsetting data and logical operators {background-color="#dc354a"} ## Our first wrangling function: `filter()` . . . `filter()` **subsets** data objects based on **rules** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](img/filter.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: . . . ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} baby_subset <- babynames %>% filter(name == "Angel") ``` ::: Subset `babynames` to only babies named `Angel` # Why filter? {.center background-color="#dc354a"} ## Why filter? {.center} . . . Lots of real-world **applications**: finding flights, addresses, IDs, etc. . . . Sometimes we want to focus on a specific **subset** of data: the South, Latin America, etc. . . . Useful to deal with common problems: outliers, missing data, strange responses ## Using `filter()` To use `filter()`, we need to tell R which **observations** we want to include (or exclude) using *rules* . . .
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} gap_africa = gapminder |> filter(region == "Africa") ``` ::: Rule: return all observations from `gapminder` where the `region` variable **is equal to** "Africa" ## Making the rules: logical operators ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} - Rules filter data based on whether **variables** meet certain criteria - Rules rely on **logical operators**: - Equal to, not equal to, less than, more than, included in, etc. - Observations that meet the rule are returned; those that are not are **dropped** ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](img/ben.jpeg){fig-align='center' width=90%} ::: ::: ::: ::::: ## The logical operators ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} | Operator | meaning | |:--------:|:-----------------------------:| | == | equal to | | != | not equal to | | > | greater than | | < | less than | | >= | greater than or equal to | | <= | less than or equal to | | & | AND (both conditions true) | | | | OR (either condition is true) | | %in% | IN (in the set of) | ::: ::: ::: notes Why double equal sign? ::: ## Using `filter()` Say we have some data on 🍎 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |name |color | pounds|sweet | |:------------|:-----|------:|:-----| |Fuji |red | 2|TRUE | |Gala |green | 4|TRUE | |Macintosh |green | 8|FALSE | |Granny Smith |red | 3|FALSE | ::: ::: ## Apples ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} apples ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 4 name color pounds sweet 1 Fuji red 2 TRUE 2 Gala green 4 TRUE 3 Macintosh green 8 FALSE 4 Granny Smith red 3 FALSE ``` ::: ::: ::: callout-note The output reports how many rows and columns our dataset has (4 rows x 4 columns) ::: ## Green apples ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} apples |> filter(color == "green") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 4 name color pounds sweet 1 Gala green 4 TRUE 2 Macintosh green 8 FALSE ``` ::: ::: . . . Notice words are in quotations! . . . Notice that the number of rows has decreased: `2 x 4` ## Green and unsweet apples ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} apples |> filter(color == "green") |> filter(sweet == FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 4 name color pounds sweet 1 Macintosh green 8 FALSE ``` ::: ::: Notice TRUE/FALSE are all-caps! ## Apples that aren't green ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} apples |> filter(color != "green") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 4 name color pounds sweet 1 Fuji red 2 TRUE 2 Granny Smith red 3 FALSE ``` ::: ::: The ! symbol **negates**: *not* equal to ## At least 4 pounds but less than 6 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} apples |> filter(pounds >= 4, pounds < 6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 4 name color pounds sweet 1 Gala green 4 TRUE ``` ::: ::: Notice: **at least** implies *greater than or equal to* . . . I could also split this up over multiple `filter` calls ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} apples |> filter(pounds >= 4) |> filter(pounds < 6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 4 name color pounds sweet 1 Gala green 4 TRUE ``` ::: ::: . . . ## Combinations: The OR (\|) operator "Observations where either *this* is true **OR** *that* is true" . . . Apples that are red OR green ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} apples |> filter(color == "red" | color == "green") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 4 name color pounds sweet 1 Fuji red 2 TRUE 2 Gala green 4 TRUE 3 Macintosh green 8 FALSE 4 Granny Smith red 3 FALSE ``` ::: ::: ::: callout-note The \| should be above your Return/Enter key ::: ## Combinations: the AND operator (&) The `&` operator can be used to combine rules . . . Returns observations where *both* rules are true . . . "Apples that are red AND sweet or green AND sour": . . . ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} apples |> filter(color == "red" & sweet == TRUE | color == "green" & sweet == FALSE) ``` ::: ## %in% The `%in%` operator is super powerful . . . It returns observations that belong to a **set** . . . Say I wanted to look at just South American countries, normally: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} gapminder |> filter(country == "Argentina" | country == "Brazil" | country == "Chile") ``` ::: Brutally repetitive ## %in% Make a list of countries and return observations that match any of them ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} keep = c("Argentina", "Brazil", "Chile") gapminder |> filter(country %in% keep) ``` ::: ::: callout-note To make a "list" of items (a **vector**), use `c()` ::: ## 👑 World leaders Example 👑 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(juanr) ?leader leader |> filter(country == "VNM" & yr_office <= 1 & age == 11) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 16 country gwcode leader gender year yr_office age edu mil_service combat 1 VNM 815 Thanh Th… M 1889 1 11 Seco… 0 0 # ℹ 6 more variables: rebel , yrs_exp , phys_health , # mental_health , will_force , will_force_sd ``` ::: ::: ## 👑 Cars Practice 👑 Open an r script, open the code book to find the variable names, and filter to find the car model. Next Using the `mtcars` dataset, identify: 1. A manual car, with 6 cylinders and the miles per gallon is less than 20. ::: callout-note `?mtcars` to see the codebook. ::: ## 👑 Cars Practice Answer 👑 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mpg cyl disp hp drat wt qsec vs am gear carb Ferrari Dino 19.7 6 145 175 3.62 2.77 15.5 0 1 5 6 ``` ::: :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
